aesTools.decryptarticleintrobody1: AES decryption restores plaintext from data encrypted with the same AES key material. This tool is designed for the JSON envelope produced by the ToolTab AES Encryptor. The envelope keeps the algorithm, key derivation settings, salt, IV, ciphertext, and plaintext metadata together, while the password or raw key remains separate.
aesTools.decryptarticleintrobody2: All work happens locally with the browser Web Crypto API. The encrypted JSON, password, raw key, and decrypted result are not uploaded.
aesTools.decryptarticlenotesbody1: AES-GCM authenticates the encrypted data, so wrong keys or changed JSON should fail instead of returning altered plaintext. AES-CBC and AES-CTR can decrypt compatible envelopes, but they do not authenticate ciphertext by themselves.
aesTools.decryptarticlenotesbody2: Keep the password or raw key separate from the JSON envelope. Anyone with both the envelope and the key material can recover the plaintext. For file envelopes, the recovered download uses the original filename and media type stored in the JSON.

aesTools.encryptarticlenotesbody1: Keep the password or raw key separate from the encrypted JSON. Anyone with both the JSON and the key material can decrypt the data. If you encrypt a file, download the JSON result and keep the original filename separately if that context matters.
aesTools.encryptarticlenotesbody2: Do not reuse a manual IV with the same key. This tool generates a fresh IV and salt for each run, which is the safer default. Prefer AES-GCM unless another system specifically requires AES-CBC or AES-CTR.
aesTools.encryptarticlewhatbody1: AES is a symmetric encryption algorithm, which means the same secret is used to encrypt and decrypt the data. This tool runs entirely in your browser and uses the Web Crypto API, so plaintext, passwords, and selected files are not uploaded.
aesTools.encryptarticlewhatbody2: The default mode is AES-GCM because it encrypts and authenticates the output. Authentication matters: if the ciphertext, salt, or IV changes later, decryption should fail instead of returning altered data. AES-CBC and AES-CTR are available for compatibility, but they do not authenticate ciphertext by themselves.
aesTools.encryptarticlewhenbody1: Use it when you need to protect a note, token, configuration snippet, or small file before storing or sharing it through another channel. The output is a JSON envelope containing the mode, key derivation settings, salt, IV, and ciphertext, so those parameters stay together for the matching decrypt step.
aesTools.encryptarticlewhenbody2: For password-based encryption, the password is processed with PBKDF2 and a random salt. Increase the iteration count when you can tolerate slower encryption and decryption. For raw-key encryption, paste a hexadecimal key with exactly the selected length: 32 hex characters for 128-bit, 48 for 192-bit, or 64 for 256-bit.
aesTools.encryptcbcwarning: AES-CBC does not authenticate ciphertext. Use it only when compatibility requires it.
aesTools.encryptctrwarning: AES-CTR does not authenticate ciphertext. Use it only when compatibility requires it.

baseEncoding.base58rules: Bitcoin, Flickr and Ripple use different Base58 alphabet orders. Decoding ignores whitespace and preserves leading zero bytes; no Base58Check checksum is applied. Processing runs in a Worker and Clear cancels it. Raw data is limited to 1 MiB
baseEncoding.base64about: Base64 represents bytes as text. It is not encryption and does not protect secrets. Encoded text is roughly one third larger

baseEncoding.base16ArticleBody: Base16, also called hexadecimal (hex), is a binary-to-text encoding that represents each byte as two characters using digits 0-9 and letters A-F. It is widely used for inspecting bytes, checksums, and identifiers.
baseEncoding.base16ArticleNoteOne: Hex doubles the size of the original data: each byte becomes two characters.
baseEncoding.base16ArticleNoteTwo: This tool accepts optional 0x prefixes and ignores whitespace
baseEncoding.base16ArticleUseThree: Encoding binary data in a format that is easy to copy and paste
baseEncoding.base32ArticleBody: Base32 is useful when a text-only or case-insensitive channel needs to carry binary data, such as OTP secrets, DNS-safe tokens, or exported configuration values. It is an encoding layer, not a security layer.
baseEncoding.base32ArticleNoteOne: Base32 expands data more than Base64.
baseEncoding.base32ArticleNoteTwo: It does not encrypt or hide the original value.
baseEncoding.base32DecoderArticleNoteThree: Some systems omit = padding, but invalid characters still cause decode errors.
baseEncoding.base32DecoderArticleWhenOne: Decoding Base32 secrets or tokens back into their original bytes.
baseEncoding.base32DecoderArticleWhenThree: Checking whether pasted Base32 data has valid characters and padding before use.
baseEncoding.base32DecoderArticleWhenTwo: Inspecting values copied from TOTP setup, integration exports, or config files.
baseEncoding.base32EncoderArticleNoteThree: Some systems require = padding, while others accept unpadded output, so match the receiver.
baseEncoding.base32EncoderArticleWhenOne: Encode bytes, text, or files before sending them through text-only channels.
baseEncoding.base32EncoderArticleWhenThree: Convert raw file bytes into a copyable string for transport, logging, or manual entry.
baseEncoding.base32EncoderArticleWhenTwo: Prepare OTP secrets, exported settings, or binary blobs for systems that expect Base32 input.
baseEncoding.base58DecoderArticleAlphabetBody: Base58 is not one universal alphabet. Bitcoin, Flickr, and Ripple use different character orders. If a value fails validation or decodes into the wrong result, switch the alphabet and try again with the format used by the system that produced it.
baseEncoding.base58DecoderArticlePurposeBody: Use this tool to decode Base58 strings or text files back into their original bytes directly in your browser. It is useful when you need to inspect payloads copied from APIs, wallets, logs, QR workflows, or import and export steps without sending the data to a server.
baseEncoding.base58DecoderArticleWatchBody: The output panel shows a UTF-8 text preview when the decoded bytes can be read as text. Binary data and non-text payloads are safer to review by downloading the .bin file. Pasted whitespace is ignored, so wrapped values from emails, docs, and terminals can still be decoded.
baseEncoding.base58DecoderOutputDescription: Preview the text restored from the current Base58 input, then copy it or download the original bytes.
baseEncoding.base58EncoderArticleHelpBody: This tool encodes text or selected files as Base58 using the Bitcoin, Flickr, or Ripple alphabet. You can switch alphabets before encoding, compare output formats, and export the result without sending data to a server.
baseEncoding.base58EncoderArticleWhenBody: Use it when you need a compact text form for binary data, want to test how an address or payload changes across Base58 alphabets, or need to prepare a value for documentation, demos, interoperability checks, or offline workflows.
baseEncoding.base58EncoderArticleWhyBody: Base58 removes visually confusing characters such as 0, O, I, and l, which makes encoded values easier to copy, read, and share in URLs, wallet addresses, QR payloads, and human-reviewed identifiers.
baseEncoding.base85DecoderArticleHelpBody: This tool converts ASCII85 or Z85 text back into the original bytes directly in the browser. You can paste encoded data, import a file, switch alphabets to match the source system, preview the decoded result, and download the recovered binary without sending anything to a server.
baseEncoding.base85DecoderArticleNoteOne: ASCII85 and Z85 are not interchangeable. Choosing the wrong alphabet usually causes decode errors or corrupted output.
baseEncoding.base85DecoderArticleNoteThreeBefore: Z85 requires complete 5-character groups, while ASCII85 may also include delimiters and shorthand such as
baseEncoding.base85DecoderArticleNoteTwo: Base85 is an encoding format, not encryption. The decoded result may be plain text, compressed content, or arbitrary binary data.
baseEncoding.base85DecoderArticleWhyBody: Base85 appears when binary data has to move through text-only systems with less overhead than hexadecimal or Base64. You may encounter it in PostScript or PDF streams, ZeroMQ Z85 payloads, debugging captures, archived exports, and tools that need printable characters instead of raw binary bytes.
baseEncoding.base85DecoderUnsupported: Background Workers are unavailable. Use a modern browser with Worker support
baseEncoding.base85EncoderArticleHelpBody: This tool encodes text or selected files as Base85 using the ASCII85 or Z85 variant. You can switch variants before encoding, confirm which format the target system expects, and export the result without sending data to a server.
baseEncoding.base85EncoderArticleWhenBody: Use it when you need a text-safe representation of binary data, want to verify whether a workflow expects ASCII85 or Z85, or need to prepare payloads for copy-paste, documentation, and offline utilities.
baseEncoding.base85EncoderArticleWhyBody: Base85 packs four bytes into five printable characters, which makes it denser than hexadecimal while still being easy to move through logs, documents, PDF/PostScript streams, and debugging tools.
baseEncoding.base85EncoderInvalidBase85: Z85 requires the input length to be a multiple of 4 bytes.

blakeHash.blake2bArticleSummary: BLAKE2b is a cryptographic hash function that is faster than MD5, SHA-1, SHA-2, and SHA-3, yet is at least as secure as the latest standard SHA-3. It produces variable-length hash outputs from 8 to 512 bits (1 to 64 bytes). BLAKE2b is optimized for 64-bit platforms and is part of the BLAKE2 family developed by Jean-Philippe Aumasson, Samuel Neves, Zooko Wilcox-O'Hearn, and Christian Winnerlein.

bcryptTools.generatorArticleCostBody: Higher cost values are slower and usually safer, but they also make every login attempt slower for your application. A cost around 10-12 is common for interactive systems; higher values can be reasonable for admin-only or low-volume workflows. Test the cost on the same kind of hardware that will verify the password.

article.exampleFour: chmod 775 shared-folder is useful for team directories when the group should also be able to create and modify files.
article.exampleOne: chmod 755 script.sh gives the owner full access and lets everyone else read and execute.
article.exampleThree: chmod 600 .env is a common choice for private secrets because only the owner can read or write it.
article.exampleTwo: chmod 644 notes.txt keeps a file writable by the owner while everyone else can only read it.
article.numeric: Each numeric digit represents one role: owner, group, and others. Inside each digit, 4 means read, 2 means write, and 1 means execute. Add the values together to build the permission you want: 7 = rwx, 6 = rw-, 5 = r-x, and 4 = r--. For directories, the execute bit also allows entering the directory.
article.what: chmod ("change mode") is a Unix/Linux command for changing file and directory permissions. This calculator lets you move between numeric permissions like 755, symbolic permissions like rwxr-xr-x, and the checkbox matrix without doing the mental math by hand.

cidrTools.cidrParserArticleIntroBeforeFirst: CIDR Parser turns a block like

cidrTools.cidrParserArticleWhatBody: The result starts with a quick overview, then breaks the block into practical details: canonical CIDR, total and usable address counts, range start and end, plus the integer values behind the block. For IPv4, you also get the netmask, wildcard mask, and broadcast address. For IPv6, the parser keeps the same workflow but hides fields that do not apply.
cidrTools.cidrParserArticleWhyBody: Many pasted CIDR values include host bits. That is fine for humans, but routers, ACLs, and documentation usually need the canonical network address instead. By rewriting the block before you copy anything out, the tool makes it easier to catch off-by-one assumptions before they leak into config.

cidrTools.cidrsMergerArticleHowBody: The merge list is normalized first: host bits are cleared, overlapping networks are folded together, and adjacent networks are collapsed when they can be represented by a shorter CIDR block. After that, the exclusion list is subtracted from the merged ranges. The final output is expanded back into the minimal CIDR list that exactly covers what remains.
cidrTools.cidrsMergerArticleInputBody: Enter one CIDR per line, or separate multiple CIDRs with commas. IPv4 and IPv6 blocks can be pasted together, but exclusions only apply to blocks from the same address family. Invalid entries are reported with their list and line number so you can fix large pasted inputs without guessing.
cidrTools.cidrsMergerArticleWhatBody: This tool combines CIDR blocks into the smallest equivalent set, then subtracts any CIDR blocks you put in the exclusion list. It supports IPv4 and IPv6 in the same run, and all processing happens locally in your browser.
cidrTools.cidrsMergerArticleWhenBody: Use it when cleaning firewall rules, preparing cloud security group entries, reviewing VPN allowlists, summarizing route tables, or removing reserved ranges from a larger allocation. It is especially helpful when copied configuration contains overlapping blocks or when a broad network needs a few smaller ranges removed.

article.conversion: The converter rebuilds the MAC address with these steps:
article.how: You can convert an IPv6 address back to a MAC address only when the IPv6 interface identifier was derived from that MAC with the EUI-64 method. This is most common with older link-local addresses that start with fe80:: and some stateless autoconfigured addresses.
article.howTitle: How to convert an IPv6 address to a MAC address
article.stepFour: Format the remaining 48 bits as a standard MAC address.
article.stepOne: Read the last 64 bits of the IPv6 address.
article.stepThree: Flip the universal/local bit in the first byte.
article.stepTwo: Remove the inserted ff:fe bytes from the middle of the interface identifier.
article.why: You may not get a result for several reasons:
article.whyOne: The IPv6 address is not syntactically valid.
article.whyThree: The address uses privacy, stable-random, DHCPv6, or another non-MAC-based assignment method.
article.whyTwo: The address is valid, but it was not generated from a MAC address with EUI-64.
article.works: This reverse conversion works when the last 64 bits of the IPv6 address still contain an EUI-64 interface identifier.
article.worksOne: The interface identifier was built from a 48-bit MAC address.
article.worksThree: The address was not generated by privacy extensions or another randomization scheme.
article.worksTwo: The middle bytes are still ff:fe.

common.catalogToolUuidV3GeneratorMessagesArticl: UUID v3 is not a random ID and is not secret. Anyone who knows the namespace and name can regenerate the same UUID. Do not use it for passwords, session tokens, API keys, or other values that must be unpredictable.

UUID v3 is a name-based UUID format. It takes a namespace UUID and a name, hashes them with MD5, and formats the result as a standard UUID. The important behavior is determinism: the same namespace and name always produce the same UUID.
This tool runs entirely in your browser. The namespace, name, and generated UUID stay on your device unless you copy the result elsewhere.
Use UUID v3 when you need a stable identifier for a known name, such as a DNS name, URL, object path, or username.
Pick the namespace that matches the kind of name you are identifying. DNS and URL are the most common presets.
Reuse the same namespace consistently. Changing the namespace changes every generated UUID, even when the name stays the same.

Prefer UUID v5 or another modern identifier when you have a choice and need a name-based UUID with a stronger hash. UUID v3 exists for compatibility with systems that specifically expect MD5-based UUIDs.

pngOptimizer.articleNotesBody: Lossless PNG optimization is not guaranteed to shrink every file. Some images have already been optimized, and occasionally a different PNG layout can be the same size or slightly larger. In that case, keep the original file or try a lower compression level.
pngOptimizer.articleOptionsBody: The compression level controls how much work Oxipng performs. Lower levels return faster, while higher levels try more combinations and can take longer on large images. PNG interlacing can help older viewers show a coarse preview while loading, but it can also increase size. Alpha optimization is usually worth keeping on because it only applies lossless transparent-pixel improvements.
pngOptimizer.articlePrivacyBody: The image is processed locally in your browser. The tool creates a temporary browser object URL for preview and download, and it does not upload the PNG to a server.
pngOptimizer.articleWhatBody: The PNG Optimizer compresses PNG images with lossless Oxipng optimization. It rewrites the PNG structure, compression settings, palette data, and alpha information where possible without changing the visible pixels.
pngOptimizer.articleWhenBody: Use it before publishing screenshots, UI assets, diagrams, icons, or transparent graphics where PNG is the right output format. It is useful when you need a smaller file but cannot accept quality loss, color shifts, or conversion to a different image format.

Common image files can be previewed visually, and PDF documents open in the browser's built-in PDF viewer when available. Other binary files remain downloadable, but the tool will not try to render them.

audioRecorder.articleOfflineBody: Use the Audio Recorder to capture a quick voice note, microphone test, narration draft, or sound sample without leaving the browser. The tool requests microphone access only when you start a recording, then lets you pause, resume, stop, preview, and download the result.
audioRecorder.articlePrivacyBody: Recording happens through the browser's MediaRecorder API. Audio remains local to the page while you record and preview it; ToolTab does not upload the microphone stream. The final file type depends on browser support, so one browser may download WebM or OGG while another produces M4A.
audioRecorder.articleTipsBody: Use a quiet environment, keep the microphone input level reasonable, and make a short test take before recording something important. If the page cannot start recording, check that the site is open over HTTPS or localhost and that microphone permission is allowed for the current browser tab.
audioRecorder.articleUsesBody: It is useful for checking whether a microphone works, collecting a spoken reminder, recording a temporary pronunciation sample, or creating a short clip to attach to another workflow. Because the recorder runs client-side, it is also a convenient option when you do not want to install a desktop audio app for a simple take.

qrCodeGenerator.articleOptionsBody: The error correction setting controls how much of the QR code can be damaged or obscured and still scan. Use medium for most codes, high when the code may be printed small or placed near a logo, and low only when keeping dense data compact matters more than resilience. Keep enough quiet zone around the code, and make sure foreground and background colors have strong contrast.
qrCodeGenerator.articlePrivacyBody: Generation happens in your browser. Wi-Fi passwords, contact details, and event text stay on your device. Download PNG, JPG, or WebP for documents, slides, and chat apps; use SVG when the QR code will be scaled in design tools or printed at multiple sizes.

crcChecksumCalculator.articleIntro: CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check) checksums are compact values used to detect accidental data changes. They are common in network frames, archive formats, embedded protocols, firmware updates, and file integrity workflows where a fast error-detection value is more useful than a cryptographic signature.
crcChecksumCalculator.articleSecurity: CRC is designed for accidental error detection, not for password storage, signatures, or tamper-proof security. For security-sensitive verification, use a cryptographic hash or signature workflow instead.
crcChecksumCalculator.articleVariantsBody: The calculator supports CRC-1, CRC-8, CRC-8 1-Wire, CRC-8 DVB-S2, CRC-16, CRC-16 CCITT, CRC-16 Modbus, CRC-16 Kermit, CRC-16 XModem, CRC-24, CRC-32, CRC-32 MPEG-2, CRCJAM, and CRC-64 models including ECMA-182, GO-ISO, MS, NVME, REDIS, WE, and XZ.
crcChecksumCalculator.articleWatchBody: CRC variant names matter. The same input can produce different values depending on polynomial, initial value, reflection settings, and final XOR. If you are matching a protocol or vendor spec, choose the result whose variant name matches that spec rather than treating every CRC width as interchangeable.
crcChecksumCalculator.articleWhenBody: Use this calculator when you need to compare CRC values from documentation, hardware protocols, file formats, or another system. Paste text for quick checks, or import a file when the checksum needs to be calculated from the exact byte stream.

article.brands: Card brands are identified by their BIN (Bank Identification Number) or IIN (Issuer Identification Number), which are the first few digits of the card number.
article.luhnIntro: The Luhn algorithm (also known as Mod 10) is a checksum formula used to validate identification numbers. Here's how it works:
article.luhnStepOne: Starting from the rightmost digit, double every second digit
article.luhnStepThree: Sum all digits. If the total is divisible by 10, the number is valid
article.luhnStepTwo: If doubling results in a number greater than 9, subtract 9 from the result
article.what: Credit card validation is a process to check if a card number is potentially valid before processing a transaction. It uses the Luhn algorithm and card brand identification to verify the format.

cronExpressionGenerator.articleBody: Cron expressions are compact, but a small change in the wrong field can move a job from "weekday mornings" to "every minute." This generator gives each field its own controls so you can build a standard five-field expression without memorizing every syntax rule.

cronExpressionGenerator.articleHelps1: Start from a known preset and fine-tune one field at a time.
cronExpressionGenerator.articleHelps2: Preview upcoming local run times before pasting the expression into a scheduler.
cronExpressionGenerator.articleNotes0: This tool generates standard five-field cron: minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week.
cronExpressionGenerator.articleNotes1: Sunday is shown as `0`, which is accepted by common Unix-style cron schedulers.
cronExpressionGenerator.articleNotes2: If both day of month and day of week are restricted, many cron implementations run when either field matches. Some systems differ, so verify that combination in your target scheduler.

cronExpressionParser.articleBody: Cron expressions are compact, but a small field mistake can run a job far more often, or far less often, than intended. This parser validates the expression in your browser, explains the schedule in plain language, breaks down every field, and previews upcoming run times.
cronExpressionParser.articleFormatBody: The tool supports standard five-field Unix cron expressions: minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week. It also accepts a six-field expression with seconds at the front for schedulers that support second-level precision.
cronExpressionParser.articleNotes0: Day-of-week values commonly use `0` or `7` for Sunday, and names such as `MON` or `FRI` are also accepted.
cronExpressionParser.articleNotes1: Month names such as `JAN` or `DEC` can make production schedules easier to review.
cronExpressionParser.articleNotes2: If your scheduler uses a different cron dialect, confirm special tokens such as `?`, `L`, `W`, or `#` in that scheduler's own documentation.
cronExpressionParser.articleResultBody: The summary gives a plain-language description, while the field table shows how the raw expression is split. The upcoming run times use your browser's local time zone, so compare them with the time zone used by the scheduler that will run the job.

csrGenerator.fillItems0: Key source — pick Generate new to create a fresh key pair, or Import existing to paste an unencrypted PKCS#8 PEM key. Encrypted keys, legacy RSA PRIVATE KEY, and EC PRIVATE KEY blocks are not accepted; convert them with openssl pkcs8 -topk8 -nocrypt first.
csrGenerator.fillItems1: Algorithm — RSA is the broadest compatibility default. ECDSA produces smaller signatures and is widely supported by modern CAs and TLS clients.
csrGenerator.fillItems2: Subject — most public CAs ignore everything but the Common Name and treat the DNS SAN list as authoritative, but private CAs may still need a full DN.
csrGenerator.fillItems3: SAN entries — list the hostnames, IPs, email addresses, or URIs you want the certificate to cover. One per line, or comma-separated.
csrGenerator.fillTitle: How to fill in the form
csrGenerator.importDescription: Paste an unencrypted PKCS#8 PEM private key. Encrypted, PKCS#1, or SEC1 keys are not supported.
csrGenerator.keepItems0: The private key shown alongside the CSR is generated locally and never leaves your browser. Save it before closing the tab — without the matching private key, the signed certificate is unusable.
csrGenerator.keepItems1: Public CAs require the Common Name (or at least one SAN entry) to be a DNS name they can validate against. IP-address SANs are mostly useful for internal certificates.
csrGenerator.keepItems2: The generated private key is unencrypted. Add a passphrase with openssl pkcs8 -in key.pem -topk8 -out key-enc.pem if you need one before storing it.
csrGenerator.keepItems3: Only RSA (2048/3072/4096) and ECDSA (P-256/P-384/P-521) are supported. EdDSA is intentionally omitted because acceptance across browsers and CAs is still inconsistent.

csrGenerator.whatBody: A Certificate Signing Request (CSR) is a small PKCS#10 document that a certificate authority (CA) needs in order to issue a TLS or code-signing certificate. It bundles together the public half of a key pair, the identity you want the CA to attest to (the Subject), and any extra identifiers like DNS names or IP addresses (the Subject Alternative Names, or SAN), all signed by the matching private key.
csrGenerator.whatBody2: This tool builds the CSR entirely in your browser using the Web Crypto API and @peculiar/x509. Nothing about your key or your request is sent to a server.
csrGenerator.whenItems0: Request a TLS certificate from a public CA (Let's Encrypt, DigiCert, ZeroSSL, Sectigo, etc.) when their workflow asks you to paste your own CSR.
csrGenerator.whenItems1: Generate a CSR for an internal certificate authority — ACME-based, smallstep, EJBCA, AD CS — without trusting a hosted form.
csrGenerator.whenItems2: Re-issue a certificate with the same private key by importing an existing PKCS#8 PEM key and only signing a new CSR.
csrGenerator.certCsrDescription: Generate PKCS#10 certificate signing requests in your browser. Create a fresh key or import an existing PKCS#8 private key, fill in Subject and SAN, then download the CSR.
csrGenerator.certCsrNote: A CSR is a request, not an issued certificate. Generated private keys are unencrypted. Keep them secret; nothing is saved automatically. Imported keys must be unencrypted PKCS#8

cssBoxShadowGenerator.articleParagraph1: box-shadow is a CSS property that draws one or more shadows behind or inside an element.
cssBoxShadowGenerator.articleParagraph2: Each shadow layer combines horizontal and vertical offsets, a blur radius, an optional spread radius, and a color with alpha. Add inset to turn the layer into an inner shadow.
cssBoxShadowGenerator.articleParagraph3: Multiple layers are comma-separated, which lets you stack subtle shadows for depth, glow, or crisp edges without changing your layout.
cssBoxShadowGenerator.articleTip1: Use small offsets with larger blur values for soft elevation.
cssBoxShadowGenerator.articleTip2: Use higher opacity with lower blur values for sharper edges.
cssBoxShadowGenerator.articleTip3: Combine outer and inner shadows when you need more perceived depth.
cssBoxShadowGenerator.articleTip4: Keep the layer count modest when performance matters.

article.paragraph1: A CSS gradient is an image generated by the browser from a smooth transition between colors. Because it is computed at render time, it scales to any size without pixelation and does not require image files.
article.paragraph2: Gradients come in three types: linear (direction or angle), radial (circle or ellipse from a center), and conic (a sweep around a center). Each gradient is defined by color stops; every stop can include a position and alpha to control how the colors blend.
article.paragraph3: Multiple gradients can be layered by separating them with commas in background-image, and you can combine them with background-blend-mode for richer textures. CSS also supports different interpolation color spaces, such as oklch, for smoother perceptual transitions.
article.tip1: Linear gradients are great for lighting and directional depth.
article.tip2: Radial and conic gradients are useful for spotlights, rings, and color wheels.
article.tip3: Adjust stop positions to sharpen or soften transitions.

article.different: CUID2 is built to reduce collisions across distributed systems while staying URL-friendly. Each value starts with a lowercase letter, uses only lowercase base36 characters, and mixes counters, host fingerprints, and random entropy before hashing the final result.
article.intro: Generate CUID2 identifiers locally in your browser without sending the current batch to another service. This tool is useful when you need compact public IDs for records, URLs, invitation links, fixtures, or client-side placeholders and want direct control over both batch size and output length.
article.options: Use shorter outputs when you want tighter slugs for demos, test data, or temporary links. Increase the length when you need more headroom for long-lived records or larger workloads, and raise the count when you want to mint a whole batch in one pass.

deviceInformation.articlePrivacyBody: The tool runs entirely in your browser and does not upload the snapshot. Browsers deliberately hide or round some values, especially memory, CPU, GPU, network, and user-agent details. Missing values usually mean the browser does not expose that API, the page is not in a secure context, or a privacy setting blocked access.
deviceInformation.articleReadBody: Treat the data as the browser's current view of your environment, not a guaranteed hardware inventory. Resize the window or rotate the device, then refresh the snapshot to update viewport, orientation, and display values. Use the JSON copy action when you need to share the exact observed values with a developer or support team.
deviceInformation.articleWhatBody: Device Information collects the browser-visible details for the device you are using right now. It groups the results into browser, display, hardware, network, storage, and capability sections so you can quickly see what a website can detect without installing diagnostic software.
deviceInformation.articleWhenBody: Use it when you need to debug responsive layouts, reproduce support tickets, compare browsers, confirm whether cookies or local storage are available, check display dimensions, or capture a compact JSON snapshot for a bug report. It is also useful before testing canvas, WebGL, clipboard, service worker, or storage-dependent features.

euVatNumberValidator.articleChecks1: Format — the remaining characters must match this tool’s country-specific format rules. Belgian input uses ten digits, Austrian input starts with U and eight digits, and Dutch input supports both the legacy numeric format and the alphanumeric format handled by the local checksum rules.
euVatNumberValidator.articleChecks2: Checksum — this tool implements local checks for Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden. Some formats, including French non-numeric keys, are left unchecked.
euVatNumberValidator.articleChecksBody: Passing means the supported local checks did not fail. An unchecked checksum is not a successful checksum check. This tool does not verify registration, ownership or whether a number is currently active.

euVatNumberValidator.articleCommon0: Unsupported country codes, such as US or UK.

euVatNumberValidator.articleCommon2: Spaces, dots, or dashes that an invoicing system pasted in — the tool normalizes them away and checks the result.
euVatNumberValidator.articleCommon3: The classic Greek GR versus VAT EL mix-up, which the format check rejects immediately.
euVatNumberValidator.articlePrivacyBody: Every check runs locally in your browser. Nothing is sent to a server or logged. Your last input is saved in your browser's local storage so it remains available after a page reload.
euVatNumberValidator.articleResultBody: The result separates the country code, normalized number, expected format and checksum. “Not checked” means this tool does not implement that check or the check does not apply to the supplied format; it does not mean the algorithm is unpublished.
euVatNumberValidator.articleWhatBody: A VAT identification number is issued by an EU member state to businesses that are registered for Value Added Tax. It starts with a two-letter country code (for example, BE for Belgium or EL for Greece), followed by a country-specific sequence of digits and sometimes letters. Tax authorities use it to track cross-border trade and refund claims, so mistakes on invoices, contracts, or procurement records can easily block a payment or trigger an audit.

faviconAssetsGenerator.articlePaddingBody: Each platform has its own padding ("Margin") so you can leave breathing room inside the icon canvas. The "Add background" switch paints an opaque square behind your source — useful when the source is transparent and the destination requires opacity (Apple's home screen) or just for visual contrast in a browser tab. Maskable PWA icons use an extra safe zone on top of the platform margin: anything outside the central ~80% may be cropped by Android, Windows, or ChromeOS when they apply a circular, rounded, or squircle mask.

gifToAnimatedWebpConverter.articleLead: Animated WebP can keep the motion of a GIF while often producing smaller files for websites, product previews, documentation, and chat-friendly assets. This converter runs locally and, when you keep the default scale, speed, and loop settings, sends the original GIF through a lossless gif2webp min-size encoder before exporting .webp files.
gifToAnimatedWebpConverter.articleOptionsBody: Scale changes every frame before encoding, which is useful when a GIF is larger than the place where it will be displayed. Speed changes playback timing without dropping frames. Loop behavior can follow the source GIF, force infinite playback, or use a custom count for assets that should stop after a specific number of plays. Keeping scale at 100%, speed at 1x, and loop behavior set to Follow GIF uses the default lossless min-size path.
gifToAnimatedWebpConverter.articlePrivacyBody: The conversion runs in your browser. Lossless WebP usually compresses GIF-style animation better, but it cannot guarantee every output will be smaller; tiny or already optimized GIFs can grow because the WebP container still has overhead. Changing scale, speed, or loop behavior requires frame decoding and can use significant memory for very large GIFs. If the source GIF does not contain loop metadata, the default export plays once unless you choose infinite or custom looping.
gifToAnimatedWebpConverter.articleWhenBody: Use this tool when you have animated GIFs that need a more modern web format, especially for pages where file size and loading speed matter. Animated WebP is supported by current major browsers and can preserve transparency, timing, and looping behavior.

highwayhashHashTextOrFile.articleOptionsBody: Enter the key as exactly 32 bytes of hexadecimal data, such as 0x000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f101112131415161718191a1b1c1d1e1f. The 0x prefix is optional, and the tool accepts spaces, colons, hyphens, and underscores to make long keys easier to read. ipInfoLookup.meaningBody: Location and ISP fields come from public IP metadata providers such as geojs.io and ip.sb, while hostnames come from reverse DNS PTR lookups when available. These records describe how public databases see the address, not the exact physical location of a person or device.

Empty fields are normal for private, reserved, newly allocated, or lightly documented addresses.

article.how: A CIDR block represents a power-of-two sized network aligned on a matching boundary. When a range starts or ends in the middle of those boundaries, one block is not enough. The converter keeps taking the largest aligned block that fits, then repeats until the entire range is covered.
article.howTitle: How IP ranges become CIDR blocks
article.what: This tool converts a start IP address and end IP address into the smallest set of CIDR blocks that exactly covers the full range. Everything runs locally in your browser, so the addresses never leave your device.
article.when: Use it when preparing firewall rules, route summaries, ACL entries, cloud security groups, or migration checklists where a raw start and end range needs to become standard CIDR notation.
article.whyBodyAfter: do not start on a clean network boundary and do not end on one either. The exact result is therefore a short list of blocks, each covering one aligned portion without including extra addresses outside the requested range.

jwkPemConverter.articleParagraphs0: A JWK (JSON Web Key) represents a cryptographic key as JSON. It is used by JOSE/JWT, JWKS endpoints, and serverless or browser applications. Command-line tools and infrastructure often require PEM key files instead.
jwkPemConverter.articleParagraphs1: PEM wraps DER key data with BEGIN/END labels, which is what OpenSSL, TLS tooling, API gateways, and many SDKs usually ask for.
jwkPemConverter.articleParagraphs2: This converter bridges those formats locally in your browser. It handles RSA, EC (P-256/384/521), and OKP key containers, lets you choose public SPKI or private PKCS8 PEM when starting from JWK, and can turn supported PEM blocks back into pretty or compact JWK JSON.
jwkPemConverter.articleParagraphs3: Use public output when you only need verification or distribution. Private conversions expose private key material on screen and in downloads, so treat the result like a secret and close the tab when you are done.

jwtDecoderVerifier.articleSecurityBodyOne: JWT payloads are only encoded, not encrypted. Anyone with the token can read its claims unless the token is a separate encrypted JWE, which this tool does not process.
jwtDecoderVerifier.articleSecurityBodyTwo: Do not paste production tokens or private secrets on shared machines. The tool runs locally in your browser and does not store the token or verification material, but the safest workflow is still to use short-lived test tokens and public keys whenever possible.
jwtDecoderVerifier.articleWhatBodyOne: A JSON Web Token is a compact string with three base64url segments: a header, a payload, and a signature. This tool decodes the header and payload in your browser so you can inspect the token structure without sending it to a server.
jwtDecoderVerifier.articleWhatBodyTwo: Signature verification checks whether the token was signed with the key and algorithm you expect. Use a shared secret for HS256, HS384, or HS512 tokens. Use a PEM public key, JWK, or JWKS for RS, PS, and ES tokens.
jwtDecoderVerifier.articleWhatTitle: What is a JWT decoder and verifier?

jwtDecoderVerifier.articleWhenBodyTwo: Use verification when you have the matching secret or public key and need to confirm that the header, payload, and signature still belong together. The tool also highlights exp, nbf, and iat so common clock and expiry issues are visible immediately.

article.summary: IPv6 Link-Local addresses are special IPv6 addresses that are automatically configured on every IPv6-enabled interface. pdfSplitter.articlePrivacyParagraphs0: The PDF is processed locally in your browser and is not uploaded by this tool. Generated download links are temporary object URLs that exist only in the current tab. Review the resulting files before sharing them, because copied pages can still contain embedded metadata, annotations, form values, or hidden content from the original document.
pdfSplitter.articleRangesParagraphs0: Use comma-separated page numbers and inclusive ranges. `1-3,5,8-10` selects pages 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9, and 10. A page can appear only once in the expression, and descending ranges such as `7-4` are rejected so the output order stays clear and predictable.
pdfSplitter.articleRangesParagraphs1: For a single output PDF, the selected pages are copied into one new document in the order shown by the range expression. For multiple output PDFs, "one file per range" keeps each typed segment together, while "one file per page" creates a separate PDF for every selected page.

pgpKeyGenerator.articleHandlingBody: Download the public key, private key, and revocation certificate as separate files. Back up the private key in an encrypted password manager or secure offline storage, and keep the revocation certificate somewhere separate so you can retire the key if the private key is lost or exposed. Before publishing a public key, compare the fingerprint through a trusted channel.
pgpKeyGenerator.articleHowToGenerateBody: Enter a name, email, or both so the key has a recognizable user ID. Add an optional comment if you want to separate work, project, or release-signing keys. Choose ECC for modern OpenPGP software, or RSA when you need compatibility with older tools. A passphrase is optional, but strongly recommended for any private key you intend to keep.
pgpKeyGenerator.articleHowToGenerateTitle: How to generate a key pair
pgpKeyGenerator.articleKeyTypesBody: ECC uses Curve25519 and is the default because it is compact and fast. RSA is available at 2048, 3072, and 4096 bits for compatibility. Expiration is set in days; use 0 only for keys that you actively manage and can revoke. Shorter expiration periods reduce long-term risk and make rotation habits easier.
pgpKeyGenerator.articleSummary: Use this tool to create an OpenPGP key pair directly in your browser. It produces an armored public key, private key, revocation certificate, key ID, and fingerprint so you can set up encrypted mail, file encryption, release signing, or account recovery workflows without sending the key material to a server.
pgpKeyGenerator.articleWhenToUseBody: PGP keys are useful when you need asymmetric cryptography: other people use your public key to encrypt data for you or verify signatures, while your private key decrypts data and creates signatures. A browser-based generator is convenient for short setup sessions, demos, or local workflows where you want the result immediately.

Keep the volume low and do not wear headphones while transmitting.

ulidGenerator.articleMonotonicBody: When monotonic batch mode is enabled, IDs generated for the same millisecond increment their random segment so the batch remains lexicographically sorted from top to bottom. Disable it when you want each row to use a fresh random segment instead. Either mode keeps the timestamp visible in the first ten characters.
ulidGenerator.articleSummary: Generate ULIDs locally in your browser for records, events, logs, fixtures, and distributed systems that need compact identifiers with time-sortable prefixes. Each value is created on this device and can be copied or downloaded without sending the batch to another service.

Switch to a custom timestamp when you need deterministic-looking samples, backfilled rows, replayed events, or fixtures that should sort around a specific moment.
ulidGenerator.articleWhyBody: ULID stands for Universally Unique Lexicographically Sortable Identifier. It combines a 48-bit Unix millisecond timestamp with 80 bits of randomness, then encodes the result as a 26-character Crockford Base32 string. That shape makes ULIDs URL-safe, database-friendly, and naturally sortable by creation time.

unicodePunycodeConverter.usage: Edit either the ASCII domain or Unicode domain; the other field updates automatically in the opposite direction. Copy either value, or use Reset example to restore the sample pair.
unicodePunycodeConverter.whatIsPunycodeDescription: Punycode is a representation of Unicode using only the letter–digit–hyphen (LDH) subset of ASCII required by DNS hostnames. It is the encoding profile used by IDNA and an instance of the Bootstring algorithm (RFC 3492). In practice, ASCII characters in a label are kept as‑is and a hyphen separates them from the encoded non‑ASCII part; for use on the public Internet the ACE prefix xn-- is prepended to the label. For example, München becomes Mnchen-3ya at the code‑point level and the DNS label xn--mnchen-3ya. Conversions are exact and reversible under IDNA processing and normalization; this tool performs both directions entirely in your browser.

uuidV1Generator.articleClockBody: The clock sequence is a 14-bit value that helps avoid collisions when the same node generates IDs around the same time. Batch generation keeps all IDs in the same millisecond and increments the 100-nanosecond tick for each row, so every value in the result remains distinct.
uuidV1Generator.articleHelpsBody: UUID v1 stores a timestamp, a clock sequence, and a 48-bit node value in a standard 36-character UUID string. That makes generated IDs roughly sortable by creation time while still fitting systems that accept ordinary UUID columns, URLs, logs, and API payloads.
uuidV1Generator.articlePrivacyBody: Classic UUID v1 generation used a real network card MAC address, which can expose hardware information. This tool starts with a locally administered random MAC address instead. You can enter a specific node value when matching a legacy system, but avoid using real hardware addresses in public samples or shared data.
uuidV1Generator.articleSummary: Generate UUID v1 identifiers locally in your browser when you need values that include creation time and a node identifier. This tool is useful for legacy integrations, database imports, ordered fixtures, and systems that still expect RFC 4122 version 1 UUIDs.

uuidV1V6Converter.articlePrivacyBody: UUID v1 and UUID v6 can encode creation time and node information. Treat them as operational identifiers, not secrets, and avoid exposing them when timestamp or node metadata could be sensitive.
uuidV1V6Converter.articlePurpose: Use this tool when you need to move identifiers between systems that expect different time-based UUID layouts. Paste a UUID v1 to get its UUID v6 equivalent, or paste a UUID v6 to recover the UUID v1 representation. The conversion is deterministic and keeps the clock sequence and node bytes unchanged.
uuidV1V6Converter.articleSummary: UUID v1 and UUID v6 contain the same core information: a timestamp, a clock sequence, and a node identifier. UUID v1 stores the timestamp in the historical UUID field order, while UUID v6 reorders those timestamp bits so simple lexicographic sorting follows creation time more naturally.
uuidV1V6Converter.articleWhenOne: Migrating records from legacy UUID v1 storage to UUID v6 while preserving identity metadata.
uuidV1V6Converter.articleWhenThree: Checking whether a UUID v6 value maps back to the UUID v1 value expected by an older integration.
uuidV1V6Converter.articleWhenTwo: Debugging databases, logs, or queues that mix UUID v1 and UUID v6 values.

uuidV6Generator.articleHelpsBody: Use UUID v6 when you need identifiers that remain broadly compatible with UUID tooling but also sort close to creation order in logs, database indexes, event streams, or migration scripts. UUID v6 is closest to UUID v1 semantically: it uses a Gregorian timestamp, a clock sequence, and a 48-bit node field, but rearranges the timestamp bits so newer IDs sort after older IDs.
uuidV6Generator.articleIntro: UUID v6 Generator creates time-based UUIDs that keep the familiar UUID shape while putting the timestamp first for natural lexical sorting. It runs entirely in your browser, so generated identifiers and optional node values never leave the page.
uuidV6Generator.articlePrivacyBody: Classic UUID v1 generators often use a real MAC address as the node field. This tool defaults to a random, locally administered node ID for each generated UUID so it does not expose a hardware address. Switch to a custom node only when you intentionally need v1-compatible output for test fixtures, interop checks, or controlled systems.
uuidV6Generator.articleSequenceBody: The clock sequence helps avoid collisions when timestamps repeat or clocks move backward. The default random sequence is safest for normal use. Custom timestamps, node IDs, and clock sequences are useful for deterministic examples, but repeated custom values should be used carefully in production data.

article.title: Create calendar files in your browser
article.intro: This tool generates standard .ics event files directly in your browser. You can define timed or all-day events, choose a time zone strategy, add reminders, and export the final calendar entry without syncing any data to a server.
article.why1: Build a clean calendar invite when you only need a file, not a full calendar account workflow.
article.why2: Keep sensitive schedules local while still generating a standards-based event attachment.
article.why3: Tune recurrence rules and reminder offsets before downloading the final .ics file.
article.workflow1: Fill in the event summary, location, notes, and optional reference URL.
article.workflow2: Pick the event range, then decide whether to export UTC timestamps or preserve the original time zone with TZID.
article.workflow3: Add recurrence and reminder rules only if the event needs them, then download the file and attach it wherever you share the event.
article.note1: UTC output is usually the safest choice when you want broad calendar compatibility.
article.note2: TZID output keeps the original scheduling context for clients that understand named time zones.
article.note3: For all-day events, the form keeps the end date inclusive even though the ICS file stores it as an exclusive end date.

ipv6UlaGenerator.about: An IPv6 ULA is intended for local networks, private interconnections and VPNs. The ULA block is fc00::/7; locally assigned prefixes use fd00::/8 with the L bit set to 1. The L = 0 allocation method is not defined by RFC 4193.
ipv6UlaGenerator.compatibility: Requires Web Crypto for secure randomness. Clipboard access may require a secure browser context. Generation works locally and does not need a network connection after the tool loads.

ipv6UlaGenerator.description: Generate a local IPv6 /48 prefix using secure browser randomness and plan its /64 subnets.
ipv6UlaGenerator.facts: ULA space: fc00::/7 · Locally assigned: fd00::/8 (L = 1) · Prefix length: /48 · 65,536 /64 subnets · Random source: Web Crypto
ipv6UlaGenerator.format: This fd00 generator formats /48 and /64 output in canonical lowercase RFC 5952 notation, suppressing leading zeros and compressing the longest zero run.
ipv6UlaGenerator.instructions: Copy and record a generated /48, then enter a hexadecimal Subnet ID to plan a /64. Generate again only when you want a new candidate site prefix.
ipv6UlaGenerator.layout: The layout is fd (8 bits) + random Global ID (40 bits) + Subnet ID (16 bits) + Interface ID (64 bits). A site receives one /48 and can allocate 65,536 /64 subnets. Choose a different Subnet ID for each subnet; interface addresses are assigned separately.
ipv6UlaGenerator.name: IPv6 ULA generator
ipv6UlaGenerator.random: This RFC 4193 generator uses crypto.getRandomValues with exactly five bytes. It collects no MAC address, clock value or device identifier and sends no generation request. Independent prefixes have 2^40 possible Global IDs. For N interconnected sites, collision probability is approximately 1 − exp(−N² / 2^41); check for conflicts before joining networks. The historical SHA-1 example is not the only generation method.
ipv6UlaGenerator.record: Record and reuse your production /48. This page creates a new candidate on each visit; it does not save your prefix.
ipv6UlaGenerator.routing: ULAs are not globally reachable by default. They are not a firewall or an inherent security boundary. Filter them at site boundaries and keep them out of public DNS. They can coexist with global unicast addresses. Record one site prefix and reuse it rather than regenerating it for a deployed network.
ipv6UlaGenerator.subnetError: Enter a hexadecimal subnet ID from 0000 to ffff.
ipv6UlaGenerator.subnetHint: Enter 1–4 hex digits, from 0000 to ffff (0–65,535)
